title: WPMS/1507/2022 of EXECUTIVE ENGINEER PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT DIVISION DEHRADUN Vs RAJESH GUPTA

paras.text:
IN HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition (M/S) No.1507 of 2022
Executive Engineer, Public Works Department
& another .....Petitioners
Vs.
Sh. Rajesh Gupta ...Respondent
Advocate: Mr. I.P. Kohli, Standing Counsel for the petitioners/State of Uttarakhand.

Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
The brief genesis of the present writ petition, emanates as a
consequence of the decision taken by the District Magistrate, who vide its
impugned order dated 03.11.2021, consequent to which after conducting the
re-measurement, he has assessed the valuation of the land and the
consequential compensation, which would be payable to the land losers,
whose land was said to have been taken by the State agencies, for the
purposes of construction of road, without resorting to due process of law.
2. There had been various phases of litigation and ultimately as a
consequence of the judgment which had been rendered by the Coordinate
Bench of this Court in Writ Petition (M/S) No.592 of 2017 Rajesh Gupta vs.
The District Magistrate, Dehradun & others, the Coordinate Bench in its
judgment dated 16.05.2018, taking note of the fact that the State has acquired
the land without following the due process of law, had rendered a judgment
by making observations in para 3 of the said judgment to the effect that the
compensation, which is required to be paid to the land losers, who were the
petitioners before the Coordinate Bench, should have been given to the
petitioner under the provisions of The Right to Fair Compensation and
Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act,
2013. Relevant para 3 is extracted hereunder:-
"3. Now the petitioner has filed the present writ petition
before this Court praying that the compensation 4 should
have been given to the petitioner under the Right to Fair

2
Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. This was never
the pleading of the petitioner and there has been no
adjudication on this aspect and therefore, this cannot even
be looked into. It is an admitted fact that the petitioner has
received the compensation earlier."
3. The said judgment of the Coordinate Bench of 16.05.2018, was
carried before the Division Bench in Special Appeal No.448 of 2018 Rajesh
Gupta vs. The District Magistrate and others. The Division Bench of this
Court vide its judgment dated 12.08.2021, had set aside the judgment of
learned Single Judge of 16.05.2018 and had issued the following direction:-
"7. Therefore, the impugned order dated 16.05.2018, passed by
learned Single Judge, is set aside and with the consent of the
parties, the present special appeal is disposed of with the
following directions:
(i) The District Magistrate, Dehradun, respondent no.1 shall
re-measure the land-inquestion and after re-measurement
of the land, he shall re-calculate the value of the land-in-question according to the circle rate of the year, 2009 and 4
thereafter, the compensation shall be given to the appellant
according to law.
(ii) (ii) The District Magistrate, Dehradun, respondent no.1,
shall take decision in the matter, after giving opportunity of
being heard to the appellant, within a period of two months
from the date of production of the certified copy of this
order."
4. As a consequence of the judgment of the Division Bench dated
12.08.2021 that the learned District Magistrate, had passed the impugned
order by conducting the exercise of re-measurement and determining the
compensation, which would be payable to the land losers based on the circle
rate, in its decision of 03.11.2021, which has been put to challenge by the
State, before this Court on the pretext, that since the decision has been taken
by the District Magistrate, in pursuance to the decision of the Division Bench
dated 12.08.2021, the petitioner had been rendered remediless, as against the
decision of the District Magistrate. This Court is of the view that taking over
of a private land of an individual has had to be governed by the provision of a
statute governing the field of acquisition, may it be under the land of Land

3
Acquisition Act of 1894 or under The Right to Fair Compensation and
Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act,
2013.
5. It is an admitted case of the petitioner, that at the time when the
possession of the land was taken over for the purposes of construction of the
road no acquisition proceedings whatsoever was ever undertaken, under any
of the provisions of the Act, as aforesaid, which was ever resorted to by the
respondents. In that eventuality it was argued, that it was as alternatively
pleaded, that the taking over of land of the private individual was as a
consequence of the negotiation, which was entered into between the land
owners and the State agencies, this Court is of the view that even if the
provision of the either of the Act contemplating the acquisition proceedings is
taken into consideration, the private negotiation though is one of the mode
prescribed under the Act itself for resorting to the acquisition proceedings.
6. The grievance raised by the petitioner in the present writ petition,
as of now is as against the decision of 03.11.2021 of District Magistrate, this
Court is of the view that if the land has not been taken over, as a consequence
of the issuance of any notification of acquiring the land under the provisions
of Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 and since the act of taking over of
the land of the private individuals is a fact, which was required to be
determined by the competent authority created under the Act, the District
Magistrate himself exclusively could not have exercised its powers of re-measurement and determine the arithmetical assessment of compensation and
with all respectful disagreement with the Division Bench judgment, this
Court is of the view that the High Court, in the exercise of its powers under
Article 226 of the Constitution of India, could not have vested an authority of
measurement or determination of compensation to the Executives, contrary to
the provisions which has been prescribed under The Right to Fair
Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and
Resettlement Act, 2013. The right of determining the compensation would be
exclusively falling within the domain of consideration of the authority as

4
defined under the Act, which would mean the authority as created Section 51
of the Act of 2013. Reference may be had to Section 3(f) and Section 51 of
the Act, which are extracted hereunder:-
"3(f) ―Authority means the Land Acquisition and Rehabilitation
and Resettlement Authority established under section 51;"
51. Establishment of Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and
Resettlement Authority.-(1) The appropriate Government shall,
for the purpose of providing speedy disposal of disputes relating
to land acquisition, compensation, rehabilitation and
resettlement, establish, by notification, one or more Authorities
to be known as ―the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and
Resettlement Authority‖ to exercise jurisdiction, powers and
authority conferred on it by or under this Act.
(2) The appropriate Government shall also specify in the
notification referred to in sub-section (1) the areas within which
the Authority may exercise jurisdiction for entertaining and
deciding the references made to it under section 64 or
applications made by the applicant under second proviso to 28
sub-section (1) of section 64."
7. If Section 51 of the Act is taken into consideration, the authority
defined therein would be an authority which has been exclusively vested with
the power of determining the compensation and quantifying it and who is to
be created by virtue of a Gazette notification to be issued by the State
Government. In that eventuality, the powers could not have been divested by
a judicial order to the District Magistrate, in contravention to the provisions
contained under Section 51, to be read with Section 3(f) of the Act. Because
the judicial verdict cannot confer a jurisdiction, contrary to what has been
provided under the Act. Be that as it may.
8. This aspect as to whether even the Constitutional Courts could
confer the jurisdiction on an authority or a court which is not otherwise
vested with the powers under statute to decide the matter. There had been a
consistent opinion, which has been laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court that
the High Court or even the Apex Court for that matter in its exercise of its
plenary jurisdiction cannot vest the jurisdiction with an authority to decide
the matter, which is otherwise not falling within its domain or exercise of

5
jurisdiction which has been otherwise created under the Statute. In that
relation a reference may be had to the judgment reported in 2010 (4) SCC
393, "Manish Goel Vs. Rohini Goel", particularly as that contained in
paragraph no.14, of the judgment, which is extracted hereunder:-
"14. Generally, no Court has competence to issue a
direction contrary to law nor the Court can direct an
authority to act in contravention of the statutory
provisions. The courts are meant to enforce the rule of
law and not to pass the orders or directions which are
contrary to what has been injected by law."
9. While reiterating the principles laid down in the matters of
Manish Goel (Supra), as referred above, this aspect was once again
considered by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the judgment reported in 2012 (12)
SCC 395, "State of Bihar and another Vs. Arvind Kumar and another",
which has observed in its paragraph no.16, that the courts, tribunals and the
judiciary, while exercising their powers under the prescribed judicial process
cannot individualized or personalized, the justice or a justice dispensation
system, contrary to the law or dehors to the statutory provisions. The said
conferment of the jurisdiction, which are dehors to the statutory provisions is
impermissible even by the courts under Article 226 of the Constitution of
India. The aforesaid principles has been reiterated in paragraph no.16, of the
said judgment, in which it has been laid down on the basis of the ratio laid
down by the Manish Goel Judgment's, (supra) that the courts are normally
meant to enforce a law, and not to contravene it. The courts are not supposed
to pass an order or a direction, which are contrary to, what has been provided
under the Statute exercising the powers of adjudication by any specific
authority, the authority cannot be vested or created by the courts by issuing
any directions, as such, in the exercise of its judicial powers.
10. In the matters of "State of West Bengal Vs. Subhas Kumar
Chatterjee and others", as reported in 2010 (11) SCC 694, the Hon'ble
Apex Court, in paragraph no.30, of the said judgment, has observed, that
whether a writ of mandamus would lie for seeking a direction to compel the
State or its Agencies, to act in contravention to or contrary to the procedure
prescribed under the law. Hence, no court can issue a writ of mandamus for

6
directing the authorities to act in contravention to the Rules, and it would
amount to compelling the authorities to violate the law, such a direction may
result into a destruction of the laid down legal principles. The relevant
paragraph no.30, is extracted hereunder:-
"30. Yet another question that arises for our consideration
is whether a writ of mandamus lies compelling the State
to act contrary to law? The State Government having
accepted the recommendations of the successive Pay
Commissions gave effect to those recommendations by
framing statutory rules being ROPA Rules and scales of
the employees have been accordingly fixed. The
respondents did not challenge the vires of the said Rules
under which they were entitled to only a particular scale
of pay. The State Government is under obligation to
follow the statutory rules and give only such pay scales as
are prescribed under the statutory provisions. Neither the
Government can act contrary to the rules nor the Court
can direct the Government to act contrary to rules. No
writ of Mandamus lies for issuing directions to a
Government to refrain from enforcing a provision of law.
No court can issue a writ of Mandamus directing the
authorities to act in contravention of the rules as it would
amount to compelling the authorities to violate law. Such
directions may result in destruction of rule of law."
11. An identical issue, which was subject matter of the consideration
in a judgment reported in AIR 1974 (Supreme Court) 2089, "P. Dasa Muni
Reddy Vs. P. Appa Rao", and in paragraph no.12, of the said judgment,
which is dealing with the aspect of the jurisdiction in the matters of the rent
control as applicable to the State Government, it had observed that when the
Authority is not vested with the jurisdiction which has been created by the
statute, it cannot decide and, if any, such decision is taken by the authority
not otherwise competent under the law to decide the matter for want of
jurisdiction, the whole proceeding or the coram artificially created to decide
the matter, would be non judice, and in the absence of the conditions
necessary to confer the jurisdiction, and to make an order to be given a shape
of the decision taken by the competent court, the same cannot be divested to
be exercised in contravention to the provisions of the law. The same
principles have been reiterated in paragraph nos.14 and 15, of the said
judgment. Relevant paragraph nos.12, 14 and 15, is extracted hereunder:-

7
"12. It is indisputable that the Rent Controller could
have no jurisdiction in respect of the building in
question because of the date of construction of the
building. The decree in the suit before the Rent
Controller cannot be pleaded as res judicata because
the Rent Controller would have no jurisdiction to try
and decide not only a particular matter in the suit but
also the subsequent suit in which the issue is raised.
See Gokul Mandar v. Pudmanund 29 I.A. 196. Section
44 of the Evidence Act also supports the appellant to
show that the judgment in the suit before the Rent
Controller is delivered by a Court not competent to
deliver it. Want of jurisdiction must be distinguished
from irregular or erroneous exercise of jurisdiction. If
there is want of jurisdiction the whole proceeding is
coram non judice. The absence of a condition
necessary to found the jurisdiction to make an order or
give a decision deprives the order or decision of any
conclusive effect
14. Just as the courts normally do not permit
contracting out of the Acts so there can be no
contracting in. A status of control of premises under
the Rent Control Acts cannot be acquired either by
estoppel or by res judicata. The principle is that
neither estoppel nor res judicata can give the court
jurisdiction under the Acts which those Acts say it is
not to have. The Rent Control Acts operate in rent.
These Acts give a status to the house from which
certain legal consequences follow.
15. In the present case, the building in question is
beyond doubt outside the protection of Rent Control
Acts. The foundation of the doctrine of estoppel is that
the representation must be of existing facts and not of
mere intention (See Dawson's Bank Ltd. v. Nippon
M.K. Kaisha 62 I.A. 100. There must be a statement
of fact and not a mere promise to do something in
future."
12. Though the logic, which has been given in paragraph no.14, is
that estoppel or resjudicata cannot confer a jurisdiction under the Act,
particularly when the Act under which the proceedings are held, it
specifically provides a forum and the legal consequences, which will flow
from the adjudication made by the authority. Hence, under the garb of the fact
that there was a directions issued in the instant case by the Division Bench to
decide the matter for the purposes of determination of the compensation, in

8
fact, would be contrary to the basic principle and genesis of exercise of
inherent jurisdiction by the constitutional courts. A conferment of the
jurisdiction is a concept which is beyond the purview and scope of Article
226 of the Constitution of India.
13. In the Constitutional Bench judgment as reported in 1988 (2)
SCC 602, "A.R. Antulay Vs. R.S. Nayak & another", two larger questions
were considered by the constitutional bench in paragraph no.19, of the
judgment, and so far as the instant case is concerned, it would be more
concerned with the second question, which was answered to the effect that if
whether any direction which is given in contravention to the law, would at all
be a valid or legal in view of the specific intention of the legislation, and
whether the proceedings held thereafter would be a judicial proceedings in
the eyes of law. It has laid down that such a direction in a proceedings though
it may be binding to the authorities to whom the directions have been issued,
but it will not be immuned for correction by the courts, because the exercise
of the powers by the judicial orders by an authority which is otherwise not
empowered under the Act would be a direction in violation of Article 14 and
21 of the Constitution of India. In paragraph no.57, of the judgment of the
Constitution Bench as referred above in the matters of A.R. Antulay (Supra),
it has held that any direction issued in suppression of the jurisdiction, which
has been validly vested under the law by a statute to a competent authority
will not validate the action taken by the authority, which has been vested with
the powers to decide the matter as a consequence of the decision rendered by
the court, which happens to be in violation of the specific statutory provisions
despite of the fact that the superior court may that it is deemed to have a
general power of jurisdiction, but the law presumes that the court has to act
within its jurisdiction and frame work of law.
14. Hence, in view of the principles laid down in paragraph nos.99
and 102, of the judgment of the Constitution Bench, it is rather envisaged that
the inherent powers of the court can be exercised only to remedy a mistake of
law, but not to perpetuate a mistake of law. This was the principles which was

9
laid down by the four judges Bench in Keshardeo Chamria Vs. Radha Kissen
Chamria & others", as reported in AIR 1953, Supreme Court, page 23.
15. In view of the aforesaid principles, I am of the view that the
argument extended by the learned Standing Counsel that the Collector did
had a jurisdiction to decide the aspect of compensation payable under the Act
of 2013, based on the direction issued by the Division Bench, is not
acceptable by this Court.
16. For the aforesaid reasons, and in the wider principles which has
been laid down by the court of law. Hence, the decision of the Collector once
it lacks the very legislative jurisdiction and the decision by the Collector,
since was not falling within the definition of the "authority," who under the
Act of 2013, was held to be competent to determine and decide the aspect of
quantification of the compensation. The order passed by the District
Magistrate could not be validated merely because of the directives of the
Division Bench, and in that eventuality, when any decision taken by the
Collector, effecting the aspect of compensation, it would be referable under
the provisions of the Acquisition Act.
17. Even at this stage, if the petitioner has any grievances qua the
quantification of the compensation which has been made by the District
Magistrate after the re-measurement of the land, which has been acquired
without due process of law, the petitioner's recourse would still be open to be
agitated by seeking a reference before the "authority" under Section 64 of the
Act, and not by way of filing of a writ petition, before this Court questioning
the propriety of the order of the District Magistrate which was rendered in
compliance of the judgment of the Division Bench, which had conferred the
powers.
18. The logic behind it is that the jurisdiction of the High Court, as
well as that of the Supreme Court, is regulated and provided under Section 63
of the Act, which, includes dealing with the dispute in relation to the land
acquisition in respect of which the Collector or authority is empowered by or

10
under this Act. In fact, the aspect of measurement, determination of
compensation and is arithmetical determination, will be within the exercise of
domain of powers to the authority under the Act. In that eventuality, the
decision taken would fall to be within the ambit and scope of consideration
before the authority under Section 64 of the Act by way of seeking of a
reference.
19. Subject to the aforesaid liberty left open to the petitioner, to seek
an appropriate reference before the competent authority as notified by the
State Government under Section 51 of the Act, the writ petition under Article
226 of the Constitution of India, would not be amenable qua the grievanced
pertaining to the determination of compensation.
20. Hence, the writ petition is dismissed subject to the aforesaid
liberty.
21. Since the petitioner has been bonafidely pursuing the
proceedings, which has been initiated at the behest of the land owners, the
aspect of limitation would be liberally construed by the authority while
exercising its powers under Section 64 of the Act.
 (Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.)
 01.07.2022
Arti
